turns.text: Start with the date and the place, then a rough headcount. Everything else, food, beds, activities, depends on those three.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We're doing it at my house, in August.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then shade and drinks are your first priorities. Rent a gazebo or borrow a couple of big umbrellas.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I cook for everyone?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: I wouldn't. Ask each household to bring one dish, and you handle the main course and drinks.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My aunt will bring her famous potato salad, so at least that's covered.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Perfect. Make a simple sign up sheet so you don't end up with six desserts and no vegetables.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And sleeping arrangements?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ask who wants to stay over early. A list of nearby hotels in the group chat saves a lot of awkward asking.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My grandad is visiting and he has trouble with stairs. Our flat is on the third floor, no lift.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's tough. Is there any chance you could meet him somewhere else for most of the visit?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Not really, he wants to see where I live.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then plan for one trip up and down per day at most, and take it slowly with rests on each landing.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Could I put a chair on the landings?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a lovely idea, a folding stool on each floor gives him somewhere to pause. Just ask your neighbours first.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Good point. Anything else / to make it easier once he's inside?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Clear the walkways, add a night light near the bathroom, and keep the things he needs at waist height.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it rude to ask family to pay for their own meals when they visit?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not necessarily. It depends a lot on your family's habits and on who invited whom.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: They invited themselves / for ten days.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then it's very reasonable to share costs. You could cover breakfasts at home and split dinners out.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I bring that up without it being awkward?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Say it early and lightly, before they arrive. Something like, we'll do breakfast here, and for dinners out let's just split as we go.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if they act offended?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Stay friendly and don't over explain. Most people adjust quickly once it's clear it's normal for you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Hi. My father is coming to visit, and he has dementia, early stage. Any advice?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: I'm sorry, that's a lot to hold. Familiar routines help the most, so try to keep his meals and bedtime close to what he's used to.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: He gets confused / in new places especially.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Labels on doors can help, like bathroom and bedroom, and a light left on at night.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I plan outings?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Short ones, and quiet ones. A garden, a familiar kind of cafe, or a drive with music he likes. Avoid crowds.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And for me? I'm worried I'll get frustrated.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's normal. Build in time for yourself each day, even twenty minutes, and ask a friend to take over for an afternoon if you can.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My partner's parents are visiting and I want to make a good impression. I'm a bit nervous.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's natural. Do you know much about them, what they enjoy or care about?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: His mum loves gardening and his dad is / into old cars, I think.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Great, those are easy openers. Ask her for advice on a plant, and ask him about the first car he ever owned.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I bring them a gift?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Something small is nice. A plant cutting for her, or a coffee table book about classic cars for him.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And at dinner, what if I run out of things to say?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ask about your partner as a kid. Parents love telling those stories, and you'll learn something too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do you split time fairly when both sets of parents want you for the holidays?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A lot of couples alternate years, one family gets the main day and the other gets the next big holiday.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We tried that. My mother still keeps score.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then maybe make it about something other than the calendar. Invite both families to yours one year, so nobody's the guest.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Both families together? / I'm not sure they'd survive.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Keep it short then, maybe a lunch instead of a whole day. Lots of food, a walk afterwards, and an easy ending time.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's actually doable.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: And whatever you pick, tell both sides at the same time. It feels fairer when nobody hears second hand.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My niece is staying with me for a week. She's six. What do I feed a six year old?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Pretty normal food, just simpler. Pasta, rice, eggs, chicken, fruit, and some vegetables she can pick at.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She told me she only eats / yellow food.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ha, that's very six. Corn, bananas, cheese, potatoes and scrambled eggs will get you far.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And breakfast? I usually just have coffee.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Cereal with milk, toast, or yogurt with fruit. Ask her parents what she normally has, kids like it to feel familiar.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Good idea. Should I let her help cook?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Definitely. Stirring, washing veggies and setting the table make kids way more likely to eat what's in front of them.

option_sets.lead_in: My parents are visiting for the first time and I need help planning their big day out.
options: The first option is a boat tour around the harbor, about two hours, with lunch included.
Then there's the art museum, which my mom would love, but my dad might get bored.
And there's a big farmers market on Saturdays with live music and lots of local food.
moshi_comment: The boat tour is a nice compromise, since it's relaxing and lunch is sorted. The museum is perfect for your mom, but you'd need something for your dad afterward. The farmers market is easy and lively, but it can be tiring if they don't like crowds.
How do your parents feel about walking and crowds? If they're easygoing, I'd do the farmers market in the morning and the boat tour after. The museum could be a short stop on another day.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm visiting my brother next month and I have to choose how to get there.
options: One way is a direct flight, only an hour, but it leaves at six in the morning.
Another is the train, about five hours, cheaper, and I could work on my laptop.
Or I could drive, which takes four hours, but then I'd have the car while I'm there.
And the last option is the overnight bus, super cheap but probably not very comfortable.
moshi_comment: The train sounds like the best balance, since you can work and it's cheaper than flying. The flight is fastest, but that early start eats up most of the time you save. Driving only makes sense if you really need a car at your brother's place.
I'd skip the overnight bus unless money is really tight. Does your brother live somewhere you can get around without a car? If yes, take the train, and if not, driving might be worth it.

option_sets.lead_in: My grandparents' anniversary dinner is on me this year and I can't pick where.
options: There's the Italian place they had their first date at, but it's changed owners and the reviews are mixed.
Or I cook at home, which is cosy, but I'd be stuck in the kitchen the whole night.
And then a fancy hotel restaurant downtown, lovely food, though Grandpa hates dressing up.
moshi_comment: The first date spot has the best story behind it, even if the food is a gamble. Cooking at home is cosy but you'd miss the moments. The hotel sounds like more about the setting than about them.
I'd go with the old Italian place, the memory matters more than the reviews. Maybe call ahead and ask if they'll do a little dessert with a candle. Home is a good backup if Grandpa's tired.

option_sets.lead_in: My mum's coming to stay and I need to figure out where she sleeps.
options: My bed, and I take the sofa, which is fine for me but I've got a bad back.
An air mattress in the study, she'd have privacy but it's a bit sad and it deflates by morning.
Or the little guesthouse two streets over, about sixty a night, with a proper bed and breakfast.
moshi_comment: With your back, a week on the sofa could leave you miserable. The air mattress saves money but she won't sleep well. The guesthouse costs a bit, but you'd both be rested and happier.
Honestly, the guesthouse sounds best, as long as she won't feel pushed out. If she would, give her your bed for a few nights and use the guesthouse for the rest.

option_sets.lead_in: We're planning a weekend away with my husband's family and I'm stuck on where.
options: A lake cabin, two hours north, with a dock and a big kitchen, but the wifi is basically nothing.
A city apartment rental, central and walkable, but we'd be squeezed into three small bedrooms.
A beach house on the coast, great for the kids, though it's a five hour drive and pricey in summer.
Or just everyone at his parents' place, free, familiar, and probably a little chaotic.
moshi_comment: The cabin feels like a real break and the big kitchen helps with a crowd, no wifi might even be a plus. The beach house is great for kids but the drive and price add up. The city place sounds cramped, and his parents' house isn't really getting away.
If there are kids, I'd pick between the cabin and the beach house. The cabin is closer and cheaper, so that's my lean. His parents' place is the easy fallback if budgets are tight.
